text: {"master_id": "jody-fisher", "work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "usage_notes": [{"chord_quality": "major", "function_role": "chord-melody-voicing", "narrative": "When arranging chord melody, find voicings that place the melody note on top of the major chord. It is often necessary to raise the melody one octave to accommodate larger major chord voicings on the fingerboard (Chapter 2, p. 9). Explore the melody in single notes across every octave before selecting a major voicing.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 2, pp. 9, 11"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "major", "function_role": "chord-family-interchangeability", "narrative": "Within the major chord family, all members--Major 6th, Major 7th, Major 9th--are functionally interchangeable; adding extensions or alterations to a basic major chord constitutes enhancement, not substitution (Chapter 2, p. 12). Context and taste should guide how much enrichment is applied, since not everything needs to be enhanced.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 12"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "major", "function_role": "over-enrichment-avoidance", "narrative": "Not every major chord needs harmonic enrichment; context is everything and taste should be the primary concern when deciding whether to add extensions to a major chord (Chapter 2, p. 12). Enriching indiscriminately undermines the musical impact of enhancement.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 12"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "major", "function_role": "subdominant-approach", "narrative": "When approaching a major I chord, it may be preceded by a IV chord--a major chord whose root is a perfect 4th higher--to handle both non-chord tones and chord tones as passing harmonization (Chapter 4, p. 39). This technique creates smooth voice-leading into the major tonic.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 39"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "major", "function_role": "same-quality-passing-chord", "narrative": "A major chord may be embellished by using another major chord a half step above or below as a passing chord, applying the same quality as the chord being approached (Chapter 4, p. 38). This like-quality passing technique is a fundamental method for chord embellishment.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 38"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "minor", "function_role": "chord-family-interchangeability", "narrative": "All chords within the minor family are functionally interchangeable; minor 7th, minor 9th, and minor 6th chords may be substituted for one another as enhancements without changing harmonic function (Chapter 2, p. 12). This enables flexible voicing selection when harmonizing a melody note over a minor chord.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 12"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "minor", "function_role": "same-quality-passing-chord", "narrative": "When approaching a minor chord, a minor chord a half step above or below may serve as a passing chord of the same quality, creating smooth chromatic voice-leading into the target minor harmony (Chapter 4, p. 38).", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 38"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "minor", "function_role": "ii-chord-in-ii-v7-i", "narrative": "The minor ii chord is a load-bearing element of the ii-V7-I progression, which defines or establishes a key through characteristic movement of roots, 3rds, and 7ths (Chapter 4, p. 40). Backcycling extends this by preceding the ii chord with its own ii-V7, repeating the fourth-movement pattern systematically.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 4, pp. 40, 44"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "passing-chord-half-step-approach", "narrative": "A dominant seventh chord--altered or unaltered--whose root is a half step higher or lower than the target chord functions as a passing chord to smooth transitions; these chords may be non-diatonic (Chapter 3, p. 23). This is one of the most common applications of passing chords in chord-melody arranging.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 23"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "tritone-substitution", "narrative": "When a progression moves from V7 to I, the V7 may be replaced by a dominant chord whose root is a tritone (diminished 5th / augmented 4th, equal to three whole steps) away, while maintaining harmonic function (Chapter 4, p. 45). This technique also applies to secondary dominant chords within a progression.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 45"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "tritone-approach-by-root-distance", "narrative": "Any chord may be approached by another chord whose root is a tritone away from the destination chord's root--this is distinct from the V7-based tritone substitution because the substitute is deduced from the destination root rather than the V7 root (Chapter 5, p. 48). This root-distance approach broadens tritone substitution beyond dominant function.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 5, p. 48"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "secondary-dominant-generalization", "narrative": "Any chord in a progression may be treated as a temporary I chord and preceded by its own V7 (secondary dominant), enhanced or altered as desired (Chapter 4, p. 39). This generalizes the V7-I principle across the entire progression, expanding the dominant's harmonic reach.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 39"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "whole-step-symmetrical-transposition", "narrative": "Dominant chord voicings that include 9ths and altered 5ths may be transposed by whole steps and still retain their dominant function, enabling harmonic color variety without changing chord quality (Chapter 6, p. 60). This symmetrical movement is a primary tool for discovering new dominant voicings from familiar shapes.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 6, p. 60"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "voice-leading-anchor-thirds-sevenths", "narrative": "The 3rd and 7th of the dominant chord are the most important tones for defining its quality and for effective voice leading, since they differentiate dominant from major and minor chords (Chapter 3, p. 22). Arrange voicings so these anchor tones move in whole and half steps between chord changes.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, pp. 21-22"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dim7", "function_role": "dominant-7th-substitute", "narrative": "A diminished chord positioned a half step below the target chord's root serves as a common substitute for the V7, because the two chords share three notes in common and both resolve similarly to the I chord (Chapter 3, p. 30). This makes the diminished a practical drop-in replacement for the dominant in chord-melody arrangements.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 30"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dim7", "function_role": "fingerboard-position-selection", "narrative": "Diminished chords repeat themselves every three frets on the fingerboard, so many possible voicing locations are available for any given diminished chord (Chapter 3, p. 28). This symmetry allows the arranger to choose the most ergonomic or voice-leading-friendly position when using a diminished as a passing or substitute chord.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 28"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "dim7", "function_role": "passing-chord-half-step-below", "narrative": "Place a diminished chord a half step below the target chord to create a smooth passing harmony that pulls convincingly toward the destination, functioning equivalently to the dominant seventh's resolution (Chapter 3, p. 30). This is a foundational move for harmonizing both chord tones and non-chord tones as passing material.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 30"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "quartal", "function_role": "alternative-harmonic-color", "narrative": "Chords constructed by stacking 4ths rather than 3rds (quartal harmony) offer an alternative harmonic color for harmonizing non-chord tones and chord tones alike in a chord-melody arrangement (Chapter 3, p. 33). Quartal voicings provide a distinct sound that contrasts with conventional tertian harmony.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 33"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "arrangement-foundation-sequencing", "narrative": "Always arrange a song with basic chords first; only after the basic arrangement is solid should harmonies be dressed up with passing chords, substitutions, and harmonizations (Chapter 2, p. 11). Applying enrichment before the structural foundation is established undermines the arrangement's coherence.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 11"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "arrangement-premature-enrichment-avoidance", "narrative": "Do not enrich or substitute chords before the skeletal arrangement is firmly in hand; building complexity on an unstable foundation prevents confident improvised harmonization (Chapter 2, p. 11). The procedural sequence--basic chords first, then passing chords and substitutions--is non-negotiable.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 11"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "skeletal-arrangement-flexibility", "narrative": "Do not carve arrangements or chord changes in stone; treat them as skeletal frameworks from which to improvise melodically, harmonically, and rhythmically (Chapter 2, p. 11). Flexibility and playfulness in performance are the goal, not fixed execution of a written score.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 11"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "non-chord-tone-harmonization", "narrative": "Non-chord tones appearing in the melody may be harmonized by adding them directly to the underlying chord as extensions or alterations, effectively renaming the chord while enhancing it (Chapter 3, p. 19). This is a primary method for generating chord enhancements organically from the melody.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 19"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "diad-harmonization", "narrative": "Both chord tones and non-chord tones may be harmonized with diads (double-stops), with 3rds and 6ths being the most common intervals (Chapter 3, p. 18). Any interval is possible but 3rds and 6ths produce the most idiomatic results in chord-melody and melodic contexts.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 18"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "octave-doubling-for-emphasis", "narrative": "Doubling melody notes in octaves creates a stronger effect than single notes, and is appropriate when melodic emphasis is desired--Wes Montgomery and George Benson are cited as authoritative models (Chapter 3, p. 36). This technique applies across all chord qualities as a melodic emphasis device.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 36"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "stepwise-voice-leading", "narrative": "Good voice leading requires that individual voices travel in whole and half steps between chord changes; prioritize the 3rd and 7th of each chord as they define quality and anchor stepwise motion (Chapter 3, pp. 21-22). Smooth voice movement is the primary criterion when selecting voicings for a chord-melody arrangement.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 3, pp. 21-22"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "voicing-position-memorization", "narrative": "Memorize chord changes and voicings in multiple areas of the fingerboard, learning them systematically in all twelve keys before applying bass-line approaches (Chapters 2 and 5, pp. 11, 50). Fingerboard flexibility across positions is essential for real-time improvised harmonization.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 11; Chapter 5, p. 50"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "minimal-finger-voicing-for-melody-freedom", "narrative": "Finger voicings with as few fingers as possible--often two--to keep additional fingers free for playing melodies and improvising (Chapter 5, p. 50). Economy of left-hand fingering is especially critical in two-part bass-line arrangements where melody must be added over chord and bass.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 5, p. 50"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "octave-voice-exploration", "narrative": "Discover new voicings by moving individual voices of familiar chord shapes to higher or lower octaves; many sounds are waiting to be discovered within shapes already known (Chapter 6, p. 60). This technique applies across all chord qualities and is the primary method for expanding voicing vocabulary without learning new shapes.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 6, p. 60"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "artistic-voice-over-accumulation", "narrative": "Knowing hundreds of chord voicings and techniques is not as important as finding your artistic voice and expressing it; how you use what you know matters more than how much you know (Chapter 6, p. 63). Voicing and technique accumulation is a means to flexibility, not the end goal.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 6, p. 63"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "reharmonization-via-bassline", "narrative": "Reharmonize sections of a tune by composing a new bass line and letting that bass line guide and drive harmonic choices (Chapter 6, p. 62). This compositional approach treats the bass line as the primary harmonic generator rather than a consequence of pre-selected chord changes.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 6, p. 62"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "triad", "function_role": "two-instrument-bass-chord-balance", "narrative": "In two-part bass-line arrangements, put a bass note on every beat and have chords appear as accented punches; maintain a realistic volume balance between bass notes and chords as if a bass player and guitarist were playing together (Chapter 5, p. 51). The two parts must remain dynamically and rhythmically distinct.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 5, p. 51"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "triad", "function_role": "bass-chord-rhythmic-delay", "narrative": "Achieve rhythmic separation in two-part arrangements by playing the bass note on the downbeat and delaying the triad chord slightly after--but within the same beat--to break up quarter-note monotony and simulate two separate instruments (Chapter 5, p. 54).", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 5, p. 54"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "triad", "function_role": "sustaining-overlapping-voices", "narrative": "Whenever possible, let two notes of the triad ring while moving to the next bass note to sustain harmonic continuity across the bass-line movement (Chapter 5, p. 55). Practice this slowly to master the physical mechanics before applying it at tempo.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 5, p. 55"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "triad", "function_role": "scale-tone-bass-connection", "narrative": "Connect triad voicings in a bass-line arrangement by using tones of the scale that the chord is built from as connective bass notes between chord positions (Chapter 5, p. 51). Scale-tone connections give the bass line melodic logic and walking-bass realism.", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 5, p. 51"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}, {"chord_quality": "triad", "function_role": "half-step-bass-approach", "narrative": "Approach any chord voicing from a note a half step above or below the lowest voice in the triad--a fundamental feature of walking bass lines that adds chromatic movement and realism to chord-melody arrangements (Chapter 5, p. 53).", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-3-mastering-chord-melody", "references": [{"source": "Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)", "citation": "Chapter 5, p. 53"}], "provenance": "extracted", "source_principle_ids": []}]}
